title: Al-'Adl, the Just
hook: the Just, who never wrongs anyone
tomorrow: thrown in a well, sold, jailed. where was the kindness?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Hakam, and a peacemaker who handed his nickname back. The line: he judges. Judging asks for something first, and that's today's Name.

Splitting a pizza between siblings. Picking teams at recess. Choosing whose group-chat message gets the quick reply. Fairness is easy when it costs nothing. The hard version shows up when your own side is the one asking for extra. Yesterday's question: fair, even against your own family? There's a verse that says yes, word for word, and a moment when the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, turned down a father who asked him to sign off on a gift.
screen: `FAIR IS EASY WHEN IT'S FREE.` → `YOUR OWN SIDE ASKS FOR EXTRA.` → `A GIFT THE PROPHET WOULDN'T SIGN.`

segments.voice: The verse first, from Surah an-Nisa, in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred." Yourselves comes first in the list. Then the father. A man named Bashir gave one of his sons, an-Nu'man, a gift, and brought him to the Prophet to witness it. Did you give each of your children the same? the Prophet asked. No. Then fear Allah, he said, and be just between your children. And the gift was taken back. That's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the Prophet declined to witness a present because a brother had been left out. Behind both stands today's Name. Al-'Adl, the Just, who never wrongs anyone. In a hadith qudsi, words the Prophet reports from Allah, Allah says He has forbidden injustice for Himself and made it forbidden among people, so do not wrong one another. The Qur'an says Allah does not wrong anyone by even a speck's weight. So fairness here isn't only a good policy. It's a reflection of who God is, practiced at the dinner table first.
screen: `EVEN AGAINST YOURSELVES.` · `ONE SON, ONE GIFT.` · `BE JUST BETWEEN YOUR CHILDREN.` · `FORBIDDEN FOR HIMSELF.` · then, large: `NEVER UNJUST.`

segments.voice: Pick one small place in your week where things run a little uneven: who always does the dishes, who always gets the front seat, whose message you always answer last. Name the fair version, name what keeps getting in the way, and choose one small step that evens it out. Then let it rest for the sit.
screen: `ONE UNEVEN PLACE.` · `THE FAIR VERSION.` · `ONE SMALL STEP.`

segments.voice: Al-'Adl. The Just, who never wrongs anyone, and who forbade injustice for Himself.
Your line: never unjust, not toward strangers and not in favor of your own. Day fifteen-oh-three, done.

howItsDone: Muslims hold that Allah is never unjust and that fairness is owed to everyone, even against oneself and one's family; parents are taught to treat their children evenly in gifts.

fork.setup: you're babysitting two little cousins. one big cookie, one small. the one you like more asks first. what does the Nu'man story point to?
options: the big one to whoever asked first; that's the rule.
the big one to the one who behaved better today.
even it out: split both, or one cuts and the other picks.
fork.reveal: be just between your children, the Prophet told a father. fairness among the small ones is where it starts, and it's a sentence a parent can say at dinner.

original.note: Arabic: the Just. listed among the Names in Jami' at-Tirmidhi.

chat.meaning: Be staunch in justice, even against yourselves or your kindred. Fair means the same scale for your side and theirs, not a thumb on either.

Al-'Adl.meaning: the Just; a Name of Allah

Surah an-Nisa.meaning: a long surah of the Qur'an, its name meaning the women

an-Nu'man.meaning: a son whose father gave only him a gift

hadith qudsi.meaning: words the Prophet reports from Allah, outside the Qur'an
